steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for a paper introducing ÌròyìnSpeech, a new Yorùbá speech corpus for TTS and ASR. Explain why African-language speakers lack voice technology, what earlier datasets did and didn't solve, and what our corpus provides.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- No voice technology for many African languages; why
- Previous large multilingual and benchmark efforts
- Yorùbá and existing Yorùbá datasets
- ÌròyìnSpeech: what it contains and provides

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem
  - many African language speakers: no voice-enabled apps in native language
  - need speech recognition + synthesis models trained on large high-fidelity speech/text data (cite)
- Prior efforts
  - large-scale multilingual datasets/models via automatic speech-text alignment (cite)
  - poor quality for low-resource African languages: few high-quality audio-text pairs, bad out-of-domain generalization
  - benchmarks for over 100 languages, high-quality but small-scale training data (cite)
- Yorùbá
  - West African, over 40 million L1 speakers, under-represented in speech research
  - several Yorùbá speech datasets (cite)
  - too small, or single speaker / single domain like BibleTTS (cite)
  - our corpus: multiple speech application domains
- ÌròyìnSpeech
  - more high quality, contemporary Yorùbá speech
  - 42 hours audio, 80 volunteers
  - text from news + creative writing, open license CC-BY-4.0
  - 5 000 sentences to Common Voice (cite) for crowdsourced recordings
  - baselines with state-of-the-art TTS and ASR
  - code + data at https://github.com/Niger-Volta-LTI/yoruba-voice

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Many speakers of African languages can't use voice-enabled applications in their native languages. One reason for this is that these technologies all need speech recognition and speech synthesis models, and those are trained on large datasets of high-fidelity speech and text.

There have been several efforts to deal with this by building large-scale multilingual datasets and models where speech and text are aligned automatically. But for low-resource African languages the results are often poor quality, because there are very few high-quality audio-text pairs and generalization out of domain is not good. Other efforts built benchmark datasets for over 100 languages with training data that is high quality but small scale.

- Yorùbá
  - West African, over 40 million L1 speakers, under-represented in speech research
  - existing Yorùbá datasets: too small, or single speaker / single domain (BibleTTS)
  - ours: multiple speech application domains
- ÌròyìnSpeech
  - 42 hours, 80 volunteers; news + creative writing, CC-BY-4.0
  - 5 000 sentences to Common Voice
  - TTS + ASR baselines; https://github.com/Niger-Volta-LTI/yoruba-voice

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Many speakers of African languages can't use voice-enabled applications in their native languages. One reason for this is that these technologies all need speech recognition and speech synthesis models, and those are trained on large datasets of high-fidelity speech and text.

There have been several efforts to deal with this by building large-scale multilingual datasets and models where speech and text are aligned automatically. But for low-resource African languages the results are often poor quality, because there are very few high-quality audio-text pairs and generalization out of domain is not good. Other efforts built benchmark datasets for over 100 languages with training data that is high quality but small scale.

This paper focuses on Yorùbá. It is a West African language with over 40 million L1 speakers, but it is under-represented in speech research today. A number of datasets have been built for Yorùbá speech tasks. These datasets are either too small to do speech processing well, or they are single speaker and single domain, like BibleTTS. Our corpus goes beyond the scope of previous work and covers multiple speech application domains.

We introduce ÌròyìnSpeech, a new dataset that we made to increase the amount of high quality, contemporary Yorùbá speech. It has 42 hours of audio in total, recorded by 80 volunteers. We curated text sentences from news and creative writing under an open license, CC-BY-4.0. We also give 5 000 sentences to the Common Voice platform so voice recordings can be crowdsourced online. We have extensive baseline experiments with state-of-the-art approaches for TTS and ASR. The code and data will be freely available on https://github.com/Niger-Volta-LTI/yoruba-voice.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Speakers of many African languages have no access to voice-enabled applications in their native languages. One reason is that these technologies all require speech recognition and speech synthesis models trained on large datasets of high-fidelity speech and text [1,2].

To address this challenge, several efforts have built large-scale multilingual datasets and models by automatically aligning speech and text [3,4,5]. However, the results are often of poor quality for low-resource African languages, due to the scarcity of high-quality audio-text pairs and unsatisfactory out-of-domain generalization. Other efforts have focused on building benchmark datasets for over 100 languages using high-quality but small-scale training data [6,7,8].

In this paper, we focus on Yorùbá, a West African language with over 40 million L1 speakers that is nevertheless under-represented in contemporary speech research. There have been a number of efforts to build datasets for Yorùbá speech tasks [9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16]. These datasets are either too small for effective speech processing or are single speaker and single domain, as in the case of BibleTTS [2]. Our corpus extends the scope of previous work to address multiple speech application domains.

We introduce ÌròyìnSpeech, a new dataset created to increase the amount of high quality, contemporary Yorùbá speech. The dataset contains a total of 42 hours of audio recorded by 80 volunteers. We curated text sentences from the news and creative writing domains under an open license, CC-BY-4.0. We also contribute 5 000 sentences to the Common Voice [17] platform to crowdsource voice recordings online. We provide extensive baseline experiments using state-of-the-art approaches for TTS and ASR. The code and data will be made freely available on https://github.com/Niger-Volta-LTI/yoruba-voice.
